incoming.name: Earthquake
incoming.excerpt: The detonation of powerful explosives, such as nuclear explosions, can cause low-magnitude ground shaking.

outgoing.name: Earthquake
outgoing.excerpt: The pressure wave from an underground explosion will propagate through the ground and cause a minor earthquake.

outgoing.name: Electromagnetic radiation
outgoing.excerpt: Nuclear weapons emit large amounts of electromagnetic radiation as visible, infrared, and ultraviolet light.

outgoing.name: Eye
outgoing.excerpt: The chief hazards are burns and eye injuries.

outgoing.name: Neutron
outgoing.excerpt: The energy of a nuclear explosive is initially released in the form of gamma rays and neutrons.

outgoing.name: Nuclear fission
outgoing.excerpt: The driving reaction may be nuclear fission, nuclear fusion or a multistage cascading combination of the two.

outgoing.name: Pythagorean theorem
outgoing.excerpt: If the effect occurs at ground zero the ground range can simply be derived from slant range and burst altitude (Pythagorean theorem).

outgoing.name: Tropical cyclone
outgoing.excerpt: The compression, vacuum and drag phases together may last several seconds or longer, and exert forces many times greater than the strongest hurricane.

outgoing.name: Ultraviolet
outgoing.excerpt: Some energy is reradiated in the ultraviolet, visible light and infrared spectrum, but most of the energy heats a spherical volume of air.

outgoing.name: Earth's atmosphere
outgoing.excerpt: …that there might be a possibility of igniting the Earth's atmosphere with a large enough nuclear explosion.
